title: We are all hypocrites
hook: people often say the church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints

segments.voice: Yesterday, church hurt: in Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away. Your line was healing takes time. Did you get to listen to someone without defending anyone? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

"They're all hypocrites." It gets said about churches at family dinners, in comment sections, sometimes with anger and sometimes with a tired shrug. And there's a reply some Christians give that surprises people: yes. All of us. A saying gets passed around about it: the church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints. Nobody seems sure who said it first, and it isn't a Bible verse. But it points at something the Bible says plainly, and says first about its own people. Today: we are all hypocrites.

Start with how Jesus uses the word in the Sermon on the Mount. He's speaking to the crowd and to his own disciples, about how they give and pray. Don't sound a trumpet when you give to the poor, he says. Don't pray on the street corners like the hypocrites, "that they may be seen of men." A hypocrite, in his picture, is someone performing goodness for an audience. Then comes the image that's almost a cartoon. "Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." A wooden beam sticking out of your face while you squint at the speck in someone else's. Some readers hear a joke in it, and then a wince. Next, Paul. He doesn't claim to have it together. In Romans he writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." The gap between what he believes and what he does is a place he lives. And he widens the circle to include everyone: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." All. That's where all of us comes from. And Jesus said who he came for: "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." So when someone says the church is full of hypocrites, a Christian who has read these texts can agree without flinching. In its own scriptures, the church was never meant to be a gallery of finished people. The danger Jesus names isn't the struggle. It's the performance: pretending the beam isn't there.
screen: `SEEN OF MEN: GOODNESS AS A SHOW.`
`THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit your hypocrisy. Settle, and breathe. Start with someone else's speck: a fault in another person that gets under your skin. Then turn the question around. Where does some version of that live in you? Or find a value you talk about but don't live. Don't punish yourself for it. Just look at the beam plainly, the way you'd look at a splinter you finally want out. Name it honestly, to yourself. If you pray, you can name it to God. The bell holds the time.
We are all hypocrites. Not an excuse but an admission: Paul's all have sinned, said with the word we.
Your line: all of us. Today, the next time you catch yourself judging someone, look for the same thing in yourself before you say a word. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Church services in several traditions include a general confession said together by the whole congregation, in which everyone, clergy included, admits their sin before God; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess privately to a priest.

fork.setup: you can clearly see a speck in your friend's eye, a small fault of theirs. according to Jesus, what comes first?
options: point it out right away, kindly.
cast the beam out of your own eye.
fork.reveal: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; then you'll see clearly to help with the speck. the speck still matters. the order is the point.

original.note: Greek: hypocrite — the word behind "Thou hypocrite" in Matthew 7:5.

trapdoor: what you thought: hypocrites are other people.
what it means: Jesus aims the word at his own listeners, and Paul says all have sinned. the church's own texts admit it.
what a scholar hears: in Matthew 6 the hypocrite does good 'that they may be seen of men'. the problem named is the performance, not the struggle.

notes: 'Hospital for sinners, not a museum of saints' is a popular saying of uncertain origin (often credited to Abigail Van Buren); the lesson says nobody seems sure who said it first and that it isn't a Bible verse. Confirm.
Matthew 6:2 and 6:5 mention the hypocrites 'in the synagogues and in the streets'; the lesson mentions only street corners so that no group becomes a foil. Confirm this is a fair summary.
Romans 7:19: readers differ on whether Paul describes his life as a believer or before faith; the lesson presents it as his own struggle without settling that. Keeper may want a note.
howItsDone 'Many church services include a general confession': soften if needed.
Original: ὑποκριτής in Matthew 7:5; the lesson avoids building on its etymology (stage actor). Confirm.
